mcqs.question: A loop increments the same counter variable a million times. Which form of locality lets the cache serve almost all of those accesses?
options: Spatial locality, because the counter is stored next to other variables
Write-back locality, a property of the cache's write policy
Temporal locality, because the same address is accessed repeatedly in a short window
Branch locality, because loops are predictable
mcqs.explanation: Repeated access to the same address is the definition of temporal locality — the counter stays resident in cache after its first fetch. Spatial locality is about nearby addresses, not the same one; "write-back locality" and "branch locality" aren't real terms.

mcqs.question: Why does a cache fetch an entire 64-byte block on a miss instead of just the requested byte?
options: Because memory buses can only transfer in fixed 64-byte chunks and that's a hardware limitation with no benefit
To simplify the cache's replacement policy
Because a single byte can't be addressed by the cache's tag bits
To exploit spatial locality — nearby bytes are likely to be needed soon, so fetching them now avoids future misses
mcqs.explanation: Fetching the surrounding block is a deliberate bet on spatial locality: code and data accesses cluster, so the neighboring bytes are often needed next and are now already resident. It's a design choice motivated by locality, not merely a bus limitation, and it's unrelated to addressing or replacement policy.

mcqs.question: If a program's memory accesses were truly uniformly random across all of RAM, what would happen to a small, fast cache's usefulness?
options: It would collapse — hit rate would depend only on the ratio of cache size to memory size, not on any reuse pattern
It would improve, since random access spreads load evenly across cache sets
It would be unaffected — caches always help regardless of access pattern
It would only affect write performance, not reads
mcqs.explanation: Caches work because real programs reuse recent data and touch contiguous memory. Strip out that locality and a cache the size of, say, 1% of RAM would hit on roughly 1% of accesses — no better than its raw capacity ratio predicts, since there's no pattern left to exploit.

mcqs.question: A column-major scan over a large 2D array is slow due to poor spatial locality. Why doesn't upgrading the machine to have 4x the RAM fix this?
options: It does fix it — more RAM means more of the array fits in memory at once
More RAM increases capacity further down the hierarchy but doesn't change the access pattern's stride, so the cache still misses on nearly every access
RAM size directly determines cache hit rate, so more RAM always helps
It only matters if the array no longer fits in RAM at all
mcqs.explanation: The bottleneck is the stride between successive accesses relative to the cache line size, not RAM capacity. Whether there's 8 GB or 128 GB of RAM behind the cache, a column-major walk still jumps past most of each fetched line before reusing it — the fix is reordering the loop or tiling, not adding memory.
